This is Chapter Five, Danish cultural life, Episode One: literature, from the runes to the Romantic poets.
In Denmark, culture and everyday life belong together.
The towns, the landscape, the schools, the technology, the science, the art, and the ways Danes meet each other have come about through a long cultural history.
Danish culture has roots back to the time when the first people settled here.
You can still find jewellery and everyday objects from the oldest times and sense the life that was once lived in Denmark.
In the landscape we see traces of the oldest burial mounds and large fortress sites.
The culture of the kings and the nobility also stands out, with castles and manor houses everywhere in Denmark.
The lives and everyday lives of the broad layers of the population have also, through many centuries, marked the country's culture.
Their work has shaped the landscape, and the culture and manners in workplaces in Denmark.
In more recent times, when the welfare state really developed in the second half of the 1900s, it was considered important to strengthen cultural life, science and art.
An active cultural life was regarded as the precondition for the individual's well-being.
Art and culture were seen as the basis of democracy, and art was allowed to provoke and question accepted truths.
Even though not everyone often goes to the theatre or reads many books, art and culture create a social life that benefits the whole population.
The welfare state has therefore promoted cultural life, and thereby also helped make Denmark internationally known within several art forms.
This chapter covers six areas: literature, visual art and sculpture, music, architecture and design, performing arts, and film.
Not all important artists are mentioned.
Danish art history has traces all the way back to the Stone Age.
Here is pottery in the form of the so-called Skarpsalling vessel, which was made around 3,200 years before Christ.
The oldest literature in Denmark is written in Old Norse with runes, the letters of the Viking Age.
The word "runes" means "secrets", and the runes were often attributed magical power.
The best-known Danish rune inscription is on Harald Bluetooth's Jelling stone from the second half of the 900s.
Here King Harald tells that he won all of Denmark and Norway for himself and made the Danes Christian.
The runic script spread all over the Nordic region, where in some places it was used long after the Latin letters were introduced.
A large part of the literature of the Middle Ages was written in Latin.
That also applies to Saxo's Danish history, Gesta Danorum, "The Deeds of the Danes", from the beginning of the 1200s.

The work was meant to show that Denmark was a country in its own right, independent of the Germans, and that Denmark's king at the time, Valdemar the Great, who reigned from 1131 to 82, was the country's rightful ruler.
Saxo tells Danish history with drama, imagination and humour.

Another important work from early literary history is King Christian the Fourth's daughter Leonora Christina's description of her prison stay, Jammers Minde, "Memoirs of Misery", written in 1673 to 74 and published in 1869.
Here she describes her long imprisonment and the accusations against her of treason.
She tells how she struggles to find meaning in life, and how she keeps an eye on everything that goes on around her.
The most prominent Danish-Norwegian author of the 1700s and the Enlightenment was Ludvig Holberg, who lived from 1684 to 1754.
Holberg wanted to promote the Enlightenment's ideals that, through enlightenment, tolerance and critical thinking, people could become freer and better human beings.
He wrote, among other things, satirical plays, comedies.
One of the most famous is Jeppe på Bjerget, "Jeppe of the Hill", from 1722, where the alcoholic Zealand peasant Jeppe is tricked into believing he is a lord of the manor.
Jeppe awakens the audience's sympathy when he asks himself why he drinks, and tells how he is beaten by his wife.
But you also look critically at Jeppe, since as a lord of the manor he is just as much a tyrant as those who usually have the power.
Danish literature from 1800 to today includes several world-famous authors.
Andersen, who lived from 1805 to 75 and was born in Odense.
He became especially known for his fairy tales, which have delighted both children and adults in Denmark and the rest of the world for almost two centuries.
The fairy tales have been translated into over 125 languages.
Den lille havfrue, The Little Mermaid.
Den grimme ælling, The Ugly Duckling.
Kejserens nye klæder, The Emperor's New Clothes.
Den lille pige med svovlstikkerne, The Little Match Girl.
These are among the most read.
Andersen's fairy tales have also inspired Disney's animated films, among other things the film The Little Mermaid from 1989, which Disney in 2023 remade in a new version.
His fairy tales are written for several age groups at the same time.
On the one hand, they contain the fantasy and supernatural world of children's stories.
On the other hand, they deal with subjects that are important to adults: prejudice, poverty, snobbery and double standards.
Adam Oehlenschläger, who lived from 1779 to 1850, was one of the best-known poets of National Romanticism.
National Romanticism wanted to promote everything that is particularly Danish in culture, nature and history.
Oehlenschläger wrote one of Denmark's two national anthems, "Der er et yndigt land", "There is a lovely land", in 1819.

Another of his best-known works is the poem "Guldhornene", "The Golden Horns", from 1802, which is about the discovery of two beautiful golden horns from antiquity, which were later stolen and melted down.

Steen Steensen Blicher, who lived from 1782 to 1848, was one of the first Danish authors to write about people's lives in what was then the distant and unknown Jutland, far away from the capital and the town.
He told about the thoughts, hopes and values of peasants, priests, civil servants, travelling traders and the poor.

He is known, among other things, for Brudstykker af en Landsbydegns Dagbog, "Fragments of a Village Sexton's Diary", from 1824, where the main character, a poor young man, tells about his modest life, his dreams and his unhappy love for a girl from the nobility whom he cannot have.

This is Chapter Five, Episode Two: literature, from the Modern Breakthrough to the middle of the 1900s.
At the end of the 1800s, Danish writers decided to shake things up.
The so-called "Modern Breakthrough", det moderne gennembrud, at the end of the 1800s wanted to break with National Romanticism and society's traditions.
The authors tried to challenge the attitudes of the day to, for example, religion, culture, family life and gender roles, which until then had been taken for granted.
Among the most important new works of the time is Herman Bang's Ved Vejen, "By the Roadside", from 1886.
The works describe experiences concerning gender and society that the age preferred to forget and avoid talking about.
Another main work from this period is Henrik Pontoppidan's Lykke-Per, "Lucky Per", from 1898 to 1904.
His great novel is about Per, who has grown up in the countryside in a priest's family with traditional values.
He goes to Copenhagen and experiences the modern society's possibilities with, among other things, industry and science, but also a new rootless existence.
Per has big dreams and plans for a modernisation of Denmark.
Pontoppidan received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1917.
Martin Andersen Nexø, who lived from 1869 to 1954, wrote especially books about poor people and their fight for better working conditions and living conditions.
Particularly well known are the novels Pelle Erobreren, "Pelle the Conqueror", from 1906 to 10, and Ditte Menneskebarn, "Ditte, Child of Man", from 1917 to 21.
Both novels have later been made into films.

The author Emma Gad, who lived from 1852 to 1921, wrote a number of plays about the questions of the day such as gender roles, morals and politics, which were performed at the Royal Theatre and other Copenhagen stages.
Emma Gad also thought that people, through clear rules, should be helped to be together without conflict.
She is therefore first and foremost known for "Takt og Tone – Hvordan Vi Omgås", "Tact and Tone: How We Get Along", from 1918, which is the best-known Danish book about how one should behave.
The book contains a number of very concrete pieces of advice about what to do in almost every imaginable situation in everyday life.

For example, you must not put your elbows on the table or put the knife in your mouth when eating, men should lift their hats when they greet, and children must not interrupt adults, but only answer kindly and politely when spoken to.
In the Danish literary history of the 1900s, Johannes V.
Jensen, who lived from 1873 to 1950, and Karen Blixen, who lived from 1885 to 1962, are some of the most appreciated authors.
Jensen's best-known novel is Kongens Fald, "The Fall of the King", from 1901, a historical novel about sixteenth-century Denmark.
It tells about King Christian the Second's futile fight to keep power as king.
Christian the Second reigned from 1513 to 23.
It is about brutality, ambitions and the beginning of Denmark's gradual decline to a small state towards the 1800s.
Another main work by Johannes V.
Jensen is Himmerlandshistorier, "Himmerland Stories", from 1898 to 1910, which is a collection of shorter stories about peasants and poor people in Himmerland in Jutland, where Johannes V.
Jensen was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Karen Blixen's best-known work is Den Afrikanske Farm, "Out of Africa", from 1937.
It is about her experiences in Kenya in the first decades of the 1900s, which at that time was a British colony.
Blixen tells here about life on her coffee farm.

She is on the one hand marked by the European colonial masters' way of thinking, but on the other hand she is critical of the colonial masters and their treatment of the African population, and she tries to arrange life on her farm in a different way.
Her work expresses her love for and respect for Africa's peoples, culture and nature.
She also tells the tragic love story she herself experiences with an English man.
Karen Blixen published, in both Danish and English, a series of stories about human passions, longings and dramas of life, which have made her known all over the world.

Tove Ditlevsen, who lived from 1917 to 76, grew up in a poor working-class family in Vesterbro in Copenhagen, and she dreamed already as a child of becoming a poet, even though her father said that girls could not become that.
She wrote poems, novels and short stories about being a child, a woman and poor in the society of the time, and among her main works is Barndommens Gade, "Street of Childhood", from 1943.

Tove Ditlevsen has in recent years, long after her death, also become popular abroad, especially in the USA, Great Britain and Germany, where her memoir series, Barndom, Ungdom og Gift, "Childhood, Youth and Dependency" in the English editions, from 1967 to 71, has been published in new translations.
Among the authors of the 20th century, Klaus Rifbjerg, who lived from 1931 to 2015, was one of the most productive.
Best known is the novel Den kroniske uskyld, "The Chronic Innocence", from 1958, which tells about the youth of society and school life.
The novel's blunt and funny criticism of school and the narrow-mindedness of adults has made it popular with generations of young readers.

This is Chapter Five, Episode Three: Danish literature from the 1960s to today.
The middle of the 1960s was characterised by a development in Danish literature that went in many new directions, with authors such as Suzanne Brøgger, born 1944.
While Suzanne Brøgger largely wrote novels about women's liberation, a number of other authors were inspired by rock music, youth rebellion and popular culture.
Another striking poet was Inger Christensen, who lived from 1935 to 2009.
Her poem "Sommerfugledalen", "Butterfly Valley", from 1991, is regarded as one of the great works in recent Danish literature.
Inger Christensen's works have been translated into many languages.
She was mentioned several times as a strong candidate for the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Naja Marie Aidt, born 1963, also began her writing as a poet, but has since also written novels and short stories.
Her best-known work is Har døden taget noget fra dig, så giv det tilbage.
Carls bog, "If Death Has Taken Something From You, Give It Back: Carl's Book", from 2017, about the grief over her young son's tragic death.
Michael Strunge, who lived from 1958 to 86, got many young readers in the 1980s for his poems about dreams, depression, love, rebellion and city life.
His main work is Verdenssøn, "Son of the World", from 1985.
One of Michael Strunge's later readers was Yahya Hassan, who lived from 1995 to 2020, was a poet, a digter, and made his debut with the poetry collection Yahya Hassan in 2013.
The collection sold in a record print run of far over 100,000 copies, and is the best-selling poetry collection in Denmark ever.

Hassan's poems about growing up and youth life as an immigrant in a ghetto neighbourhood created a violent debate, because they pointed to serious social problems and to clashes between Danish norms and the norms in socially burdened immigrant environments.
One of today's striking Danish authors is Helle Helle, born 1965.
Her toned-down descriptions of everyday life in Denmark's smaller towns mix humour, seriousness, sorrow and joy.
With the novel Rødby-Puttgarden from 2005, she broke through to a bigger audience.
Rødby-Puttgarden depicts the young sisters Jane and Tine's everyday life in Rødbyhavn on Lolland, where they both work as shop assistants on the ferry to Puttgarden.
In recent years Helle Helle has published the novels about Hafni.
In the novel Hafni fortæller, "Hafni Tells", from 2023, a woman goes out on a carefully planned journey through Denmark to celebrate her divorce.
She eats lots of open sandwiches and meets the people of the provinces.
But everything goes wrong, and the journey, which was only supposed to last eight days, ends up taking a month, because Hafni wants to change herself, but does not know how.

Some years later, in the novel Hey Hafni from 2025, we meet Hafni again, where she has travelled to the town of Brighton on England's south coast to find happiness again, which also turns out not to be so simple.
A popular genre in contemporary literature is so-called auto-fiction, where the author describes experiences from their own life and mixes them with fictional elements.

Among the themes are growing up in smaller communities, growing up in a dysfunctional family, and not "belonging", when you are caught between prejudice and traditional norms on the one side and the wish to live out your own ambitions and feelings on the other.
Leonora Christina Skov, born 1976, wrote Den, der lever stille, "The One Who Lives Quietly", in 2017.

It is about the author's upbringing on the narrow path of virtue, "to live quietly", and about the wish to win love and recognition from parents who can almost always find and magnify problems in what she does.
When she has to admit that she is lesbian, she is faced with the choice between living out her feelings on the one hand and losing her parents' acceptance on the other.
Thomas Korsgaard, born 1995, and Glenn Bech, born 1991, both likewise write from experiences of being in a family and in an environment where it is not appreciated to stand out.
Furthermore their memoirs take their starting point in a childhood and youth in families with social and psychological problems.

In the novel trilogy Hvis der skulle komme et menneske forbi, from 2017, En dag vil vi grine af det, from 2018, and Man skulle nok have været der, from 2021, Thomas Korsgaard tells, with both seriousness and irony, about the upbringing he experienced, with lack of money, education, love, and with physical and psychological violence as part of the upbringing.
Glenn Bech's debut book Farskibet, from 2021, describes the trauma his father's suicide has given him.
At the centre of the book is a family that is ruined by what Glenn Bech calls "toxic masculinity".
That is, a view of being a man that involves dominating, intolerant and violent behaviour.
A masculinity that was impossible for the father to live in, difficult for himself to be homosexual in, and which also shows itself through the mother's violent boyfriends.

Glenn Bech is not only a critic of norms about gender and sexuality but also of the city's elites, who are accused of lacking knowledge of the provinces and of the many less privileged population groups in society.
This criticism is expressed not least in his political pamphlet Jeg anerkender ikke længere jeres autoritet, "I No Longer Recognise Your Authority", from 2022.
Suzanne Brøgger, born 1944, and Naja Marie Aidt, born 1963, are both authors, forfattere.
Yahya Hassan was a digter, a poet.

This is Chapter Five, Episode Four: visual art and sculpture.
Let's start with a treasure from the Bronze Age.
The oldest examples of visual art and decoration of objects in Denmark go far back in time.
The most important treasure from the oldest times is the so-called Solvognen, the Sun Chariot, a figure that represents the sun being pulled by a horse.
The Sun Chariot dates from the older Bronze Age, about 1350 before Christ.
In the religion of that time the sun was worshipped, and the Sun Chariot shows how the sun was pulled across the sky during the day by one of its helpers, a horse.
A snake, a fish and two ships led the sun through the rest of the hours of the day and night.
The Sun Chariot is made of gold and bronze.
It was found in Trundholm Mose in North West Zealand.
In 1639 and 1734, a big gold find was made in the form of the golden horns from Gallehus in South Jutland.
They were decorated with many figures and with runes.
The golden horns date from about 400 after Christ.
They were stolen and melted down in 1802.
They have been recreated on the basis of drawings, but details of the decoration are uncertain.
With the introduction of Christianity in Denmark from the 900s, church art comes to Denmark.
It mixes with the Viking Age's decorations with human and animal figures.
This can be seen, among other things, on Harald Bluetooth's Jelling stone from the second half of the 900s, where Jesus is shown as a strong and victorious Viking warrior.
The many newly built churches of the Middle Ages, roughly 1050 to 1500, were equipped with wall paintings, kalkmalerier, which functioned as a kind of comic strips.

The paintings were to help ensure that the large majority of the population, who could not read the Bible and did not understand Latin, which was the language of the church until the Reformation, could also grasp the message of Christianity.
An example is the wall paintings of Bible stories in Birkerød Church north of Copenhagen.
After the Reformation in 1536, it was especially the king and the nobility who used art to show their wealth and importance.
The many impressive works of art at Kronborg in Helsingør demonstrate the king's power, including 40 woven tapestries showing Danish kings.

Christian the Fourth had a particularly great interest in art and culture and had several well-known foreign painters come to Denmark to paint the king and his family, and to decorate the king's many castles.
With the introduction of absolutism in 1660 to 61, power was centralised in the king.

To be able to educate Danish artists who could measure up to those abroad, Frederik the Fifth, who reigned from 1746 to 66, founded the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts at Charlottenborg at Kongens Nytorv in Copenhagen, where it still has its home.

A work from this period which is regarded as a high point in Danish art history is the French Jacques-François-Joseph Saly's equestrian statue of Frederik the Fifth from 1771, which stands in the middle of Amalienborg Palace Square and is regarded as one of Europe's most beautiful equestrian statues.
The statue by the way cost more to erect than Amalienborg's four palaces put together.
The first half of the 1800s has been given the name the Golden Age, Guldalderen, because Danish culture, art and science flourished with several internationally known names.
Andersen, who lived from 1805 to 75, the philosopher Søren Kierkegaard, 1813 to 55, who lived in the 1800s, the physicist H.C.
Ørsted, 1777 to 1851, the poet Adam Oehlenschläger, 1779 to 1850, and N.F.S.
A famous artist from the Golden Age is Bertel Thorvaldsen, who lived from 1770 to 1844, and is the best-known sculptor in Danish history.
In 1797 he travelled to Italy and lived in Rome for many years.
Here he created, inspired by the art of the Roman Empire, a series of sculptures, among other things the tomb monument of Pope Pius the Seventh.
His sculptures got their own museum, Thorvaldsens Museum, which is in Copenhagen.
The museum opened in 1848 and was the first museum building in Denmark that the population had access to.
Here are exhibited Thorvaldsen's sculptures as well as his own collection of paintings and art objects from ancient antiquity about 2,000 years ago.
Eckersberg, who lived from 1783 to 1853, is one of the most important artists from the Golden Age.
Eckersberg, among other things, went on a study stay in Rome with Thorvaldsen.
He worked with motifs from the landscape and the folk life around Rome.
In the time after, painters such as Vilhelm Hammershøi, who lived from 1864 to 1916, have marked Danish visual art.
Vilhelm Hammershøi has not least been appreciated by posterity for his ability to paint light and shadow in the rooms of a home.
His painting "Interiør fra Strandgade 30" was painted in the year 1900 and depicts the painter's wife Ida, who stands reading in the couple's home in Christianshavn in Copenhagen.
The painting was in 2023 sold at an auction in the USA for 62.8 million kroner, and thereby became the most expensive Danish painting ever sold.
Other significant painters from the same period, kunstmalere, are P.S.
Krøyer, who lived from 1851 to 1909, and the married couple Anna Ancher, 1859 to 1935, and Michael Ancher, 1849 to 1927, who belong to the circle of the so-called Skagen Painters.
Towards the end of the 1800s, a number of painters settled in Skagen, which is Denmark's northernmost town.
They painted both the local population's everyday life and the painters' own lives.
The light from the two seas, Skagerrak and Kattegat, which surround Skagen, came to play a special role in their pictures.
Anna Ancher's painting "Solskin i den blå stue", "Sunshine in the Blue Room", is from 1891.
The sculptor Anne Marie Carl-Nielsen, who lived from 1863 to 1945, was the first woman in the world to get a commission to make an equestrian statue of a king.

Today her equestrian statue of Christian the Ninth, who reigned from 1863 to 1906, can be seen at Christiansborg's Riding Ground, and she is also known for being behind the bronze doors in Ribe Cathedral.
Anne Marie Carl-Nielsen fought throughout her life for women's access to academic educations and for their right to exhibit works on an equal footing with male artists.
In more recent times, Asger Jorn, who lived from 1914 to 73, is among the world-famous Danish visual artists.
He helped found the international artists' group Cobra, which got its name from the artists' home towns Copenhagen, Brussels and Amsterdam.

His main work is the large painting "Stalingrad", named after the city where one of the bloodiest battles of the Second World War took place in 1942 to 43, and where the Soviet Union defeated Germany.
The battle is regarded as the turning point of the war, the beginning of the final German defeat in 1945.
Jorn worked on the picture from 1957 to 72.
The dominant colour is white-grey like the snow at the city, with red splashes everywhere, which symbolise blood.
Three of the most important visual artists in recent decades are Per Kirkeby, who lived from 1938 to 2018, Bjørn Nørgaard, born 1947, and Lene Adler Petersen, born 1944.
Kirkeby is internationally recognised for his large abstract paintings, which relate to a natural world, and his pictures have been exhibited all over the world.
Lene Adler Petersen has worked with both film, actions, graphics, painting and sculpture.

In 1969, she and her husband Bjørn Nørgaard created the action "Den kvindelige Kristus", "The Female Christ", where she walked naked through the Stock Exchange, Børsen, in Copenhagen with a cross in her hand.
The action became an icon of a new experimental and critical art aimed at capitalist and male-dominated norms.

An important newer artwork is Bjørn Nørgaard's main work consisting of 17 large tapestries, gobelins, which decorate the Knights' Hall at Christiansborg and tell the course of Danish history from the Viking Age to our time.
The tapestries were a birthday present from a number of business organisations, companies and others for the Queen's 50th birthday in 1990.
They took 10 years to make and were inaugurated on the Queen's 60th birthday in the year 2000.
Another artist who has made a mark in recent decades is the Danish-Icelandic Olafur Eliasson, born 1967.

One of his best-known works is Your Rainbow Panorama, in Danish Din regnbueudsigt, from 2011, on top of the art museum ARoS in Aarhus, which is a 150-metre-long circular glass walkway where you can look out over Aarhus in all the colours of the rainbow.

How far back does Danish music go?
The many large horns that have been preserved from the Bronze Age, which lasted from 1700 to 500 before Christ, suggest that music has been known in Denmark for several thousand years.
It is, however, not known with certainty what the beautiful so-called lurs, lurer, were used for.
They have been found in pairs, and posterity has tried to play on them, but how it is to be done is not known for sure.
In general, the information about music before the introduction of Christianity in the 900s is very sparse.
With Christianity came Catholic church music to Denmark, and after the Reformation in 1536, hymn singing, where the congregation was to sing along, became an important part of the church service.
The Reformation has therefore also been called the singing revolution, and the realm was gathered around hymnbooks that were authorised by the king and which everyone was to use.

Thomas Kingo, who lived from 1634 to 1703, Hans Adolph Brorson, 1694 to 1764, Nikolaj Severin Frederik Grundtvig, 1783 to 1872, and Bernhard Severin Ingemann, 1789 to 1862, are the most important hymn writers.

Their works range from hymns with a strong awareness that life is not eternal, that is Kingo, and a cultivation of an inward and emotional faith, that is Brorson, to hymns that praise nature, the child and life on earth as part of God's creation, that is Grundtvig and Ingemann.
Of these four, Grundtvig is the one to remember: he wrote a very large number of the hymns, salmer, in the Danish hymnbook, Den Danske Salmebog.
At the end of the 1700s and the beginning of the 1800s, several German musicians and composers immigrated to Denmark and renewed the music.

Friedrich Kuhlau, who lived from 1786 to 1832, wrote music for the national romantic festival play Elverhøi in 1828, which includes the music for the poet Johannes Ewald's "Kong Christian stod ved højen mast", "King Christian stood by the lofty mast", from 1778 to 79, one of Denmark's two national anthems and Denmark's royal anthem.
The text of "Kong Christian stod ved højen mast" was written in 1778 to 79 by Johannes Ewald, who lived from 1743 to 81.
Denmark is one of the only countries in the world to have two national anthems.
The other national anthem is "Der er et yndigt land", for which Adam Oehlenschläger wrote the text in 1819, and for which Hans Ernst Krøyer, who lived from 1798 to 1879, composed the music in 1835.
One of the best-known composers in the Højskolesangbog, the Folk High School Songbook, is Carl Nielsen, who lived from 1865 to 1931, and who had roots in a popular musical life on Funen.
With his operas, symphonies, chamber music and songs he became the most prominent Danish composer ever.
His music took its starting point in the romantic style of the 1800s, but he managed to unite the popular and the modern, and he worked with both simple and very complicated music.
Carl Nielsen was married to the sculptor Anne Marie Carl-Nielsen.

Danish jazz music has had outstanding musicians, bandleaders and composers from Leo Mathisen, who lived from 1906 to 69, to Palle Mikkelborg, born 1941, and the Danish-American Marilyn Mazur, born 1955.

In the 1960s Copenhagen was home to a number of American jazz musicians: for example Stan Getz, who sought an artistic refuge in Denmark for a period when the USA was marked by unrest and racial persecution.
In the 20th and 21st centuries, rock and pop music have had a very large audience.

Many different currents are in play, and the composer Bent Fabricius Bjerre, who lived from 1924 to 2020, became known for writing streams of melodies for films and TV series such as, for example, Matador.
Among the most important bands and musicians are Gasolin, Anne Linnet and TV2.

Gasolin, with the lead singer Kim Larsen, who lived from 1945 to 2018, combined pop and rock and contributed to the Danish song treasure with songs such as "Kvinde min", from 1975, and "Hva' gør vi nu, lille du?", from 1976.
Kim Larsen had a long career as a singer and songwriter, and many of his songs are used at family parties, because he can express feelings, humour and solidarity in a simple and subtly witty way.

Anne Linnet's song "Smuk og dejlig", from 1976, is about lesbian love, and the band TV2 from Aarhus, which self-ironically called itself "Denmark's most boring orchestra", sings about, among other things, everyday life, love and the importance of daring to live life and seize its opportunities.
Among TV2's best-known numbers is "Nærmest lykkelig".
In the 1990s the Danish-Norwegian music group Aqua had great success with their dance pop, where especially the number "Barbie Girl" was a global hit.
Aqua released two albums in their heyday, and with about 28 million CDs sold it is one of the best-selling Danish music groups ever.
In recent years, particularly the group Lukas Graham, with the lead singer Lukas Forchhammer, born 1988, at the head, has had great success both in Denmark and internationally.
The group released its first album in 2012, and the number "7 Years" is one of the highest-earning Danish numbers of the 2010s.
And Karen Marie Ørsted, born 1988, who is known under the artist name MØ, broke through with the single "Pilgrim" in 2013 and has since among other things released "Kamikaze" and "Final Song".
Together with the American band Major Lazer and the Canadian singer Justin Bieber she also released, in 2016, the single "Cold Water", which became a big international hit.
Denmark has won the Eurovision Song Contest, Det Europæiske Melodi Grand Prix, three times.
The first time was in 1963 with "Dansevise", which was performed by Grethe Ingmann, who lived from 1938 to 90, and Jørgen Ingmann, 1925 to 2015.

The second time in the year 2000, with "Smuk som et stjerneskud", "Fly on the Wings of Love", written and performed by the duo Brødrene Olsen, which consists of Jørgen Olsen, born 1950, and Niels Olsen, born 1954.
The third time was 2013, with "Only Teardrops", which was sung by Emmelie de Forest, born 1993.
In Danish: a composer is a komponist, a lead singer is a forsanger, hymns are salmer, and a national anthem is a nationalsang.
Here is your recap for Episode Five.
Grundtvig wrote a large number of the hymns in Den Danske Salmebog.
Lurs are Bronze Age horns, found in pairs; their use is not known.
The Reformation has been called the singing revolution; the first authorised hymnbook came out in 1569.
The most important hymn writers are Kingo, Brorson, Grundtvig and Ingemann.

Denmark has two national anthems: "Kong Christian stod ved højen mast", text by Johannes Ewald, which is also the royal anthem, and "Der er et yndigt land", text by Oehlenschläger from 1819 and music by Hans Ernst Krøyer from 1835.
Carl Nielsen, 1865 to 1931, is the most prominent Danish composer ever.
Gasolin, with Kim Larsen, Anne Linnet and TV2 are important pop and rock names.
Aqua's "Barbie Girl" was a global hit.
Lukas Graham's "7 Years" and MØ's "Cold Water" were international successes.
Denmark has won Eurovision three times: 1963, 2000 and 2013.

This is Chapter Five, Episode Six: architecture and design.
Architecture and design always reflect a society's possibilities, attitudes and values, and help make a country recognisable.
In Denmark there is a tradition of emphasising practical functions and simplicity.
You can see it already in the many village churches and half-timbered farms that, over several centuries up to the middle of the 1800s, were built on hilltops and in the landscape around the country.

It is also characteristic of the more exclusive properties which, inspired by Greek and Roman architecture, were built in the period from about 1760 to 1860, and which especially came to mark the cityscape of Copenhagen.
An example is Copenhagen's cathedral, Vor Frue Kirke, the Church of Our Lady, which was designed by C.F.
It was built in the years 1811 to 29.
Parts of the cathedral are shaped like a Roman temple, while the entrance is shaped like a Greek temple front.
Today, Danish architecture and design are especially associated with functionalism, which is a way of designing where emphasis is especially placed on practical functions.
Functionalism arose in the 1920s, where it first and foremost helped to improve the poor housing standard of the towns.
In the many decades that followed, functionalism in architecture came to mark the building and shaping of the Danish welfare state, for example many Danes' homes.

One of the ideas of functionalism was that if you removed ornaments, decorations, from, for example, houses and furniture, and made them more alike and simple in expression, you also reduced their association with particular classes in society.
Functionalism's political agenda was the wish for more social equality.
In that way functionalism has become an expression of the broad Danish middle class and its modern lifestyle.
An example of functionalism is Aarhus University, which was built in 1931 to 33.
The idea behind the university was to create a kind of academic village marked by openness and harmony, and by the wish to integrate the university's many purposes into a whole.
In University Park lie the buildings that house the individual institutes such as, for example, law, history, music and political science.
But the park also contains halls of residence, a lake and streams.
Other examples of functionalism are Poul Henningsen's lamps and Børge Mogensen's furniture.

Poul Henningsen, who lived from 1894 to 1967, also called PH, was a social commentator, revue writer, film producer and architect, but became most famous for his lamp design, which made electric light glare-free.

The lamp consists of three shades, whose sizes, materials and colours can be combined in countless variations, so that the lamp creates both a pleasant and practical lighting for different purposes and prices.

In the 1940s, Børge Mogensen, who lived from 1914 to 72, developed a functionalist-influenced furniture programme for the supermarket chain FDB, now Coop, which was similarly flexible and likewise came to mark both Danish homes and town halls, schools and hospitals with a simple expression.
Arne Jacobsen, who lived from 1902 to 71, has also made a great mark on both architecture and design.
He was inspired by several different styles, not least functionalism.
Examples of his architecture are Denmark's National Bank in Copenhagen and Aarhus City Hall.
Examples of his design are the chairs the Seven, 7'eren, and the Egg, Ægget, as well as the Stelton coffee and teapots and other kitchen and serving equipment.
Danish architecture and design are today marked by great diversity and global outlook.
The architect Jørn Utzon, who lived from 1918 to 2008, was a pioneer of this development when he in the late 1950s designed the iconic opera house in Australia's biggest city, Sydney.
The building is shaped like large upright shells covered with a pattern of white tiles.
From different angles it can resemble, for example, a cathedral, sails on a ship or the waves of the sea.
This paved the way for a more experimental, expressive and playful building style, which has met great international recognition.
Currently it is continued, among others, by Dorte Mandrup, born 1961, who is behind buildings such as the Icefjord Centre at the Ilulissat Icefjord in Greenland and the Wadden Sea Centre in Ribe.
Dorte Mandrup's style is characterised by the surroundings inspiring and shaping the buildings.
Both the Icefjord Centre and the Wadden Sea Centre clearly interact with the landscapes' special characteristics and history.
Furthermore, the architect Bjarke Ingels, born 1974, and his studio BIG, Bjarke Ingels Group, have designed several prestige buildings both in Denmark and abroad.
This applies for example to Amager Bakke, also called Copenhill, which was inaugurated in 2019.
It functions both as an energy-efficient waste incineration plant and a recreational oasis with a ski slope, hiking route and climbing wall.
Functionalism, in Danish funktionalismen, is the word to remember.

Copenhagen's cathedral, Vor Frue Kirke, was designed by C.F.
Functionalism arose in the 1920s, with the political aim of more social equality.

Bjarke Ingels, born 1974, and BIG designed Copenhill, Amager Bakke, inaugurated in 2019.

This is Chapter Five, Episode Seven: the performing arts.
The performing arts, scenekunst, include a number of different genres: drama, ballet, opera, musical and revue.
What the different genres of the performing arts have in common is that they are performed here and now in front of an audience.
And as is the case with other art forms, Danish performing arts are also inspired from abroad.
In the 1700s, the Danish-Norwegian Ludvig Holberg, who lived from 1684 to 1754, was encouraged to write comedies for the theatre.
He became so gripped by the work that in a few years he wrote 25 comedies, where fun is made of citizens, peasants and noble people.
Often it is a clever maidservant who thinks up a plot against the unreasonable people of the comedy.
One of the most performed comedies is Erasmus Montanus from 1723, where the student Rasmus travels from Copenhagen home to his old parents and his waiting fiancée and boasts about his Latin learning.
Holberg was the first to write comedies in Danish, and the comedies are still often played on Danish stages.
At the beginning of the 1800s, the performing arts were renewed.
The Romantic poets used drama to express great passions and feelings.
They found motifs in history, in folk tales and folk songs.

Exotic and fairy-tale material was also important, and the leading National Romantic poet, Adam Oehlenschläger, was inspired by the Arabian tales of One Thousand and One Nights when in 1805 he wrote the fairy-tale play Aladdin eller Den Forunderlige Lampe, "Aladdin or the Wonderful Lamp", about the young boy Aladdin, who gets hold of an old lamp that turns out to be able to fulfil all his wishes.
The play is set in Middle Eastern surroundings, but is also a description of people and types in the Copenhagen of the time.
It was sought after among authors to write for the theatre.
Drama was regarded as the most distinguished art form.
The Royal Theatre, Det Kongelige Teater, became an important cultural institution.
Johan Ludvig Heiberg, who lived from 1791 to 1860, together with his wife Johanne Luise Heiberg, 1812 to 90, was prominent here.
He became director and author for the stage, while she was an admired actress.
They made themselves noticed not least within the French-inspired genre vaudeville, where drama and music are united in comedies, often about love entanglements among the young of the middle class.
In the time of Oehlenschläger and Heiberg, ballet became a leading part of the performing arts.
The choreographer August Bournonville, who lived from 1805 to 79, produced his version of an Italian ballet, La Sylphide, Sylfiden, which was first performed at the Royal Theatre in 1836.
His choreography is the only one that has survived.
Sylfiden is thereby one of the world's oldest surviving ballets.
Sylfiden has a romantic plot about a young Scottish man, James, who on his wedding day runs away with a sylph, that is, an invisible woman of air.
Bournonville has internationally had enormous importance for ballet as an art form.
His tradition was continued and renewed in the 20th century.
Flemming Flindt, who lived from 1936 to 2009, has also helped give Danish ballet great reputation abroad.
Together with the rock musicians in Savage Rose he created, for example, the ballet Dødens triumf, "The Triumph of Death", in 1971.
The ballet delighted with its strong criticism of a society on its way to doom, and it also caused outrage when several dancers performed naked.
In January 1939, eight months before the Second World War started, Kjeld Abell, who lived from 1901 to 61, had his play Anna Sophie Hedvig premiere at the Royal Theatre.
The play is about the teacher Anna Sophie Hedvig, who during a visit to her family in Copenhagen tells that she has killed the cruel and tyrannical headmistress Mrs Møller.
Anna Sophie Hedvig is a political play, where Kjeld Abell indirectly calls for resistance to fascism and Nazism.
The poet-priest Kaj Munk, who lived from 1898 to 1944, and who was murdered by Nazis in 1944, wrote his drama Niels Ebbesen when he had settled accounts with his own sympathies for Nazism.
The play is based on a folk song about the young Jutland nobleman Niels Ebbesen, who in 1340 kills one of the great German counts to whom Denmark was pawned.
The play was printed and banned in 1942 and only performed in 1945.
With the story of Niels Ebbesen Munk wanted to rouse Danes to resistance against Nazism and the German occupying power.
It was not only in plays, but to a great extent also through the revues that artists expressed resistance to Nazism.

Even though censorship was introduced during the occupation, the revue writer Poul Henningsen succeeded in smuggling a call to resistance into Kjeld Abell's revue Dyveke, from 1940, where Liva Weel, who lived from 1897 to 1952, sang Poul Henningsen's song "Man binder os på mund og hånd", "They bind us hand and mouth".
It was apparently a song about free love, but the audience could not be in doubt that the message was resistance and solidarity around ideals of freedom.
The text was later sung and released by the band Outlandish in 2004.
Danish performing arts after the Second World War have made themselves felt within different genres.
A forerunner of today's stand-up comedy was the Danish-American Victor Borge's shows, who lived from 1909 to 2000, with comedy and music.
He had great success in the USA with his one-man show Comedy in the Music, which was performed over 800 times on Broadway in New York from 1953 to 56.

In the 1960s and 70s, TV theatre became popular, especially with Leif Panduro's dramas, who lived from 1923 to 77, about conflicts in the family and between generations in a period of growing prosperity in Denmark.
People gathered around the TV screens when Panduro's plays were shown.
One of the best is Farvel Thomas, from 1968, about a man who ends up in a deep crisis and loneliness when he gets divorced.
Line Knutzon, born 1965, has since the 1980s and 1990s helped renew the art of drama.
Her drama is satirical, socially critical and very funny.
It is especially her ability to make lines absurd and crazy that makes her plays come alive.
Her first bigger success is the play Først bliver man jo født, from 1994, which takes place among residents in a stairwell of apartments.
The musical genre, which combines traditional drama and dialogue with music and dance, became popular from the end of the 1970s and onwards.
The musician and composer Sebastian, born 1949, has written music for some of the genre's biggest successes on Danish ground such as Skatteøen, from 1986, and Ronja Røverdatter, from 1991.
The last is based on a story by the Swedish children's book author Astrid Lindgren.
And with the popularity of the stand-up genre in the present, the performing arts have got new genres that appeal to a large audience.
In so-called stand-up comedy, the comedian stands on the stage and tells jokes and entertaining stories directly to the audience.
Among the best-known Danish stand-up comedians are Casper Christensen, born 1968, Anders Matthesen, born 1975, and Nikolai Stokholm, born 1990.
Here is your recap for Episode Seven.
Performing arts include drama, ballet, opera, musical and revue.
Holberg wrote 25 comedies, and was the first to write comedies in Danish; Erasmus Montanus is from 1723.
The Heibergs were prominent at the Royal Theatre.
August Bournonville's Sylfiden, first performed in 1836, is one of the world's oldest surviving ballets.
Flemming Flindt created Dødens triumf in 1971.
Kjeld Abell's Anna Sophie Hedvig premiered in January 1939.
Kaj Munk, murdered by Nazis in 1944, wrote Niels Ebbesen.
Poul Henningsen smuggled a call to resistance into the 1940 revue Dyveke, sung by Liva Weel.
Victor Borge's Comedy in the Music ran over 800 times on Broadway from 1953 to 56.
Leif Panduro wrote Farvel Thomas in 1968.
Line Knutzon, Sebastian's musicals, and stand-up comedians Casper Christensen, Anders Matthesen and Nikolai Stokholm round out the picture.

This is Chapter Five, Episode Eight: film, from the silent era to the 1980s.
A number of Danes have, in the course of time, become internationally famous as film actors or as directors.
Around the year 1900, the first films were recorded in Denmark.
After that, the Danish film industry grew quickly and became known in many countries.
Asta Nielsen, who lived from 1881 to 1972, was Denmark's first film star.
She had great success with roles in silent films and recorded many films in Germany in the first half of the 1900s.
She was celebrated for her erotic charisma and her ability to express the whole range of feelings on the screen.
Dreyer, who lived from 1889 to 1968, is the most important director in the older Danish film history.
Films such as Vredens Dag, "Day of Wrath", from 1943, and the French La passion de Jeanne d'Arc, "The Passion of Joan of Arc", from 1928, have secured Dreyer fame.
Dreyer's close-ups and slow film tempo distinguished his films.
His film Ordet, "The Word", from 1955, is based on a drama by Kaj Munk, and the film culminates in a scene where a young mother is awakened to life from the dead.
Dreyer depicts the gripping miracle with an outstanding use of close-ups and cuts.

Early film classics are, in addition, Astrid Henning-Jensen, who lived from 1914 to 2002, and Bjarne Henning-Jensen, 1908 to 95, with Ditte Menneskebarn from 1946, after the novel by Martin Andersen Nexø; Johan Jacobsen's, who lived from 1912 to 72, Soldaten og Jenny, "The Soldier and Jenny", from 1947; and Henning Carlsen's, who lived from 1927 to 2014, Sult, "Hunger", from 1966, after the novel of the same name by the Norwegian author Knut Hamsun.
The three films have poverty and exclusion as themes and are based on novels and plays respectively.
Ditte Menneskebarn takes place at the beginning of the 20th century and is about a poor girl who is born outside marriage and is exposed to violence and abuse.
She also becomes pregnant herself without being married and is trapped in the vicious circle of poverty.
Soldaten og Jenny depicts the relationship between a young woman and a soldier who meet by chance in a bar.
Jenny has previously had an abortion, which at that time was forbidden, and is now threatened with punishment and exclusion.
Henning Carlsen's Sult takes place at the end of the 1800s and is about a young writer who wanders around Norway's capital Kristiania, today's Oslo.
He has been thrown out of his rented room and has no money for food.
He tries to pawn his few belongings, even his glasses and the buttons on his clothes, and he humiliates himself to get a job.
His situation becomes more and more desperate, all the while he moves among the city's citizens as if he had no problems.
The period from 1950 to 1975 was a heyday for commercial folk comedies.

The biggest success and Denmark's most seen film became Alice O'Fredericks's, who lived from 1899 to 1968, and Jon Iversen's, 1889 to 1964, film version of Morten Korch's, 1876 to 1954, novel De røde heste, "The Red Horses", from 1950.
The film tells the dramatic story of how a young farmer saves his farm from falling into the hands of villains by winning a big horse race.
Erik Balling, who lived from 1924 to 2005, learned from the folk comedies and delighted audiences with the film series Olsen-banden, "The Olsen Gang", of a total of 14 films, the first from 1968.
The films are inspired by cartoons and are about a fictional Danish criminal gang.
With Egon Olsen as leader, the gang has big, cunning plans to commit a heist that will make them millionaires, but which mostly goes completely wrong in a way that you have to laugh at.
The film series was copied in Norway and Sweden and was popular, in German, in the communist East Germany.
Erik Balling was also a much used director on TV.
The TV series Matador takes place in Denmark of the 1930s and 1940s.
The setting for the story is the fictional Zealand provincial town of Korsbæk.
We follow its inhabitants and experience their family life, careers, love and struggle with gender roles.
The norms of the time and important historical events are described.
The series' 24 episodes were first shown on television in 1978 to 82 and have later been rebroadcast countless times.
Matador is the most watched TV series in Denmark ever.
The script was especially written by the author Lise Nørgaard, who lived from 1917 to 2023.
Many events in the series are inspired by her own childhood and youth.
Films for children are an important part of Danish film art.
Busters Verden, "Buster's World", from 1984, by Bille August, born 1948, is a classic within this genre.
Busters Verden is based on a novel by the popular children's book author Bjarne Reuter, born 1950.
In the film we meet Buster, who has a hard time both at home and at school, where he is always bullied.
But his imagination and talent for magic help him through many of the difficulties.
In 1982, the Folketing gave Danish children's films better financial conditions, and thereby recognised the artistic importance of the children's film genre.
Excellent films about children and young people, which were also for adults, were also produced.
Nils Malmros, born 1944, directed, for example, a long series of films about young people, among others Kundskabens træ, "The Tree of Knowledge", from 1981.
The film is about bullying and crushes in a class of pubescent children.
Some friends are shut out of the community, and romantic relationships begin and end very suddenly.
The adults, both the teachers at the school and the parents, do not understand the young people's lives and their relationships with each other.
Many cinema-goers, young as well as adult, often recognised themselves in Malmros's depiction of early youth.
In Danish: an actor is a skuespiller, a film director is a filminstruktør, and a TV series is a tv-serie.
Here is your recap for Episode Eight.
The first films were recorded in Denmark around 1900, and Nordisk Film was founded in 1906.
Asta Nielsen, 1881 to 1972, was Denmark's first film star.
Dreyer, 1889 to 1968, is the most important older director, with Vredens Dag in 1943, La passion de Jeanne d'Arc in 1928, and Ordet in 1955, based on Kaj Munk.
Ditte Menneskebarn from 1946, Soldaten og Jenny from 1947, and Sult from 1966 have poverty and exclusion as themes.
1950 to 1975 was a heyday of folk comedies; De røde heste from 1950 is Denmark's most seen film.

Erik Balling made 14 Olsen-banden films, from 1968, and the TV series Matador, shown 1978 to 82, with 24 episodes, set in the fictional town of Korsbæk; it is the most watched series ever, with scripts by Lise Nørgaard.
Busters Verden from 1984 is a children's film classic; in 1982 the Folketing improved conditions for children's films.
Nils Malmros made Kundskabens træ in 1981.

This is Chapter Five, the final episode, Episode Nine: Dogme 95, and Danish film and TV today.
Dogme 95 was a manifesto which the directors Lars von Trier, born 1956, and Thomas Vinterberg, born 1969, in 1995 wrote together with Søren Kragh-Jacobsen, born 1947, and Kristian Levring, born 1957.
The four "dogme brothers" committed themselves to making simple films with focus on the good story rather than technical effects.
Dogme 95 caused a stir, and several dogme films became big successes with both audiences and critics in Denmark and abroad.

Lars von Trier's first dogme film was Idioterne, "The Idiots", from 1998, which is about a group of adults who want to provoke their surroundings and fulfil themselves by playing "idiots", that is, mentally disabled people.
The film reveals in a humorous and tragic way both the group's self-absorption and the surroundings' lack of tolerance.
Lars von Trier also won, in 2000, the Palme d'Or, Den Gyldne Palme, for the musical film Dancer in the Dark, from 2000, which had the Icelandic singer Björk in the lead role.

Thomas Vinterberg's family drama Festen, "The Celebration", from 1998, won the jury's special prize, Prix du Jury, at the film festival in Cannes in France in 1998, while another of his films, Druk, "Another Round", from 2020, won an Oscar in 2021.
In Druk, four upper secondary school teachers try to make themselves and their lives more exciting by drinking, so that they have alcohol in their blood all day.
It goes well in the beginning, but gradually it gets out of control and ends in a tragic accident.
But it is also a film about letting go of control in one's life, waking up, feeling life, starting to live again, and what consequences that can have.
The accident in the film is, for Thomas Vinterberg, a consequence of feeling life.
The directors Gabriel Axel, who lived from 1918 to 2014, Bille August and Susanne Bier, born 1960, have also received international recognition.

Gabriel Axel won, as the first Danish director, an Oscar for the film version of Karen Blixen's story Babettes Gæstebud, "Babette's Feast", from 1987, in 1988, about how a strict Christian congregation, which denies the good things of life, one day is served a lavish meal and therefore suddenly becomes happier and better people.
Bille August won both an Oscar and the Palmes d'Or for the film Pelle Erobreren, from 1987.
The film is based on Martin Andersen Nexø's world-famous novel from the beginning of the 20th century.

Susanne Bier has won both an Oscar and a Golden Globe for Hævnen, "In a Better World", from 2010, which focuses on in which situations in life it is respectively right and wrong to take revenge on others.
One of the 21st century's most prominent actors is Mads Mikkelsen, born 1965.

Mads Mikkelsen received the award for best male actor at the Cannes Film Festival in 2012 for the role in Jagten, "The Hunt", from 2012, as the teaching assistant Lucas, who is falsely accused of paedophilia.
He is ostracised by everyone in the village, and soon he has neither work, friends, girlfriend nor son.

In addition he plays one of the four upper secondary school teachers in Druk, where the uninspiring, insecure and unengaged history teacher Martin wakes up beyond recognition once he gets alcohol in his body.
He regains his joy in work and with it also the self-confidence that anew engages and motivates the pupils' interest in the subject.

Kaj has been on cash benefit for many years, consistently neglects the municipality's activation offers and spends most of the day's hours on a bench in a social housing estate in a Copenhagen suburb in the company of lots of beer, spirits, cigarettes and the neighbourhood's other alcoholics.

Kaj has a daughter whom he has not seen for 20 years, and when she one day by chance moves into the building, he suddenly stands face to face with his past, his lack of sense of responsibility and his wasted life.

Sofie Gråbøl, born 1968, is one of Denmark's best-known actresses, skuespillere, and has played several lead roles as somewhat insecure, awkward people.
She became truly known in the 1986 film version of Tove Ditlevsen's novel Barndommens Gade in the lead role as the 14-year-old Ester, who grows up in Vesterbro in the interwar period.
Ester feels caught between childhood and adult life.

Between, on the one side, the working class's hard living conditions and the expectations of women at the time, and on the other side the dream of breaking free of the known world and becoming something greater.
In the film Der kommer en dag, from 2016, which takes place at a sadistic boys' orphanage at the end of the 1960s, she plays the teacher Lillian.

When you talk about Sofie Gråbøl, the TV series Forbrydelsen, "The Killing", from 2007 to 12, cannot be avoided.

Here she appears in the role as deputy chief inspector Sarah Lund, who is to solve the murder of a 19-year-old woman.

Another of Denmark's most acclaimed actors is Trine Dyrholm, born 1972.
She has among other things taken part in Hævnen, where she plays the role as Marianne, whose husband has been unfaithful, and whose oldest son is bullied at school.
The role as the wife who feels let down by her husband also recurs in Kollektivet, from 2016.

The free-spirited Anna is, in line with the 1970s' ideals, sceptical of the nuclear family and a supporter of free love, but wakes up to reality when her husband falls in love with a younger colleague.

Another highlight in Trine Dyrholm's career, and another film about broken ideals, is Dronningen, from 2019, in the role as the lawyer Anne, who works with commitment to defend children and young people against sexual abuse, but throws her own morals overboard when she seduces her 17-year-old stepson.
